hints.title: Avoid adding symmetry
hints.body: Perpendicular diagonals specify an angle, not how the intersection divides their lengths. Draw four vertices on two perpendicular lines.
hints.recap: A right-angle crossing need not be a symmetry axis.
hints.pitfall: Do not automatically draw a kite or rhombus.
hints.pause: Put the two vertices on opposite sides at unequal distances from each axis.

recall.reminder: A universal geometry claim needs proof or an allowed counterexample.

hints.title: Choose a test quadrilateral
hints.body: Try vertices (−1,0),(0,2),(3,0),(0,−1) in that order; verify the two diagonals meet at right angles.
hints.recap: Coordinates can supply an exact test instead of relying on appearance.
hints.pitfall: Reflection must exchange off-axis vertices exactly.
hints.pause: Check whether either diagonal is a symmetry line.

recall.reminder: An exact allowed counterexample can test a universal geometry claim.

hints.title: Calculate the side midpoints
hints.body: Average the endpoint coordinates of each side to form the four midpoint vertices, then find adjacent side lengths and angles.
hints.recap: A square needs both equal sides and right angles.
hints.pitfall: A rectangle need not be a square.
hints.pause: Test the square claim on the constructed quadrilateral and classify both statements.

recall.reminder: A square needs both equal sides and right angles.

solution:
Use the quadrilateral A=(−1, 0), B=(0, 2), C=(3, 0), D=(0, −1). Its diagonals AC and BD lie on the x- and y-axes, so they are perpendicular.

Neither diagonal is a line of symmetry: B and D lie distances 2 and 1 from AC, while A and C lie distances 1 and 3 from BD. Thus I fails.

The side midpoints are (−12, 1), (32, 1), (32, −12), (−12, −12). They form a rectangle of width 2 and height 32, not a square. Thus II also fails.

Neither is necessarily true: A.
knowledgePattern: Disprove symmetry and square-midpoint claims for perpendicular diagonals
